paragraphs.text: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1F caused by NEFL mutations is a peripheral neuropathy. It typically begins early and can be severe. Nerve conduction velocities are slowed moderately to severely (Jordanova et al., 2003). The disorder can be inherited as a dominant trait through heterozygous missense mutations or as a recessive trait through homozygous nonsense mutations (Abe et al., 2009; Yum et al., 2009).

checks.explanation: NEFL-related CMT is described as a hereditary peripheral neuropathy (paper does not use the CMT1F label).

On electrophysiologic examination, nerve conduction velocities were moderately to severely slowed. The authors also reported the first nerve biopsy from a CMT patient with a de novo NEFL missense mutation. It showed axonal pathology, with axonal regeneration clusters and onion bulb formations.

paragraphs.text: Yum et al. (2009) reported a Palestinian family whose parents were first cousins. Four of their 5 children had a severe, progressive neuropathy, with onset at about 1.5 years of age. The index patient presented at age 2 years with toe walking. All 4 affected children had hypotonia in infancy and early childhood and mildly delayed motor milestones. They also had slowly progressive atrophy and weakness of the distal muscles of the feet and hands, bilateral pes cavus, moderate glove-and-stocking sensory impairment, and absent ankle jerks. One sib used a walker and had moderate proximal leg weakness and a waddling gait. Another sib had mild to moderate weakness of the proximal arm and shoulder girdle. The others walked with molded ankle-foot orthoses. CMT neuropathy scores ranged from 16 to 27. None of the children had pathologic reflexes, palpably enlarged nerves, foot ulcers, cranial neuropathies, or clinically evident hearing loss. One sib had learning difficulties. Brain MRI was normal in the 3 sibs who had it.

paragraphs.text: Sensory responses were absent in nearly all of these children (Yum et al., 2009). Median and ulnar motor conduction velocities were severely slowed, ranging from 12 to 25 m/s, and amplitudes became progressively smaller with age. Peroneal and tibial responses eventually could not be obtained in any affected child. EMG showed severe denervation in distal muscles. Visual evoked responses were prolonged in 3 of the 4 affected children, which the authors took as evidence of subclinical involvement of central nervous system axons. A sural nerve biopsy from 1 patient at age 16 years showed a reduced density of myelinated axons (1,300/mm, compared with about 6,000/mm in controls). All myelinated axons were less than 3 microns in diameter, and they contained microtubules but no intermediate filaments. There were occasional clusters of regenerated axons, but no evidence of active axonal degeneration.

paragraphs.text: Yum et al. (2009) studied the 4 affected sibs from a consanguineous Palestinian family. All 4 were homozygous for a c.628G-T transversion in the NEFL gene, predicted to result in a glu210-to-ter (E210X) substitution. Both parents were heterozygous, and the unaffected sib did not carry the mutation. Sequencing of PMP22, GJB1, MPZ, EGR2, PRX, LMNA, GDAP1, and MFN2 in 2 of the affected sibs found no additional mutations. In the patient's sural nerve, an antiserum against the N terminus of NFL labeled axons, whereas an antiserum against the C terminus did not. In SW-13 vim- cells, the E210X mutant did not form filaments. It also did not interfere with filament formation by wildtype NFL or with the vimentin network, unlike the dominant Q333P mutant. These findings suggested a simple loss of function.

paragraphs.text: Yum et al. (2009) studied 4 affected sibs from a consanguineous Palestinian family with severe, early-onset neuropathy and severely slowed nerve conduction velocities. All 4 were homozygous for a c.628G-T transversion in the NEFL gene, predicted to cause a glu210-to-ter (E210X) substitution. Both parents were heterozygous carriers, and the unaffected sib did not carry the mutation. The mutation had not been found in more than 11,000 individuals analyzed at a diagnostic laboratory. In transfected SW-13 vim- cells, the mutant protein did not form filaments, accumulated at low levels, and did not interfere with filament formation by wildtype NFL. This was consistent with a simple loss of function.
